qs.why: A higher R-value slows heat loss more.

qs.q: In many older homes, where is a good place to start?
qs.why: Warm air rises and escapes through the top of the house, and attics are often the easiest place to add insulation.

options: Stops drafts through gaps and cracks
qs.why: Moving air carries heat. Sealing gaps before adding insulation makes the insulation work better.

qs.q: What is a blower door test?
options: A fan in a doorway that shows how leaky the house is
A test of the front door's strength
A check of the roof vents
qs.why: The fan pulls air out, and gauges show how fast outside air leaks in.

qs.q: Which type of insulation is blown into an attic as loose fill?
qs.why: Loose fill spreads over uneven spaces and around pipes and wires.

qs.q: Before adding insulation, what should you fix first?
qs.why: Wet insulation stops working and can grow mould.

qs.q: After you air seal a home tightly, it also needs:
qs.why: A tighter home holds moisture and stale air unless fresh air comes in on purpose, often through a ventilator.

qs.q: Does adding insulation help in summer?
options: Yes, it keeps heat out too
No, it only works in winter
qs.why: Insulation slows heat in both directions.

qs.q: What can a home energy assessment tell you?
options: Where heat leaks and which upgrade to do first
qs.why: It ranks the fixes so your first dollar goes furthest.

qs.q: Which is a common leak in an attic floor?
options: Gaps around pipes, wires and light fixtures
qs.why: Small holes where things pass through the ceiling let warm air into the attic.
